title: In re L.E.S.
description: Whether the non-spousal artificial insemination statute (R.C. 3111.95(A)) can be judicially modified to apply retroactively to unmarried same-sex couples who would have been married but for Ohio's ban on same-sex marriage, with the plaintiff arguing it cannot and the defendant arguing it can.
plaintiff_argument: The First District erred in empowering the trial court to retroactively create a marriage under a "would have been married" standard, as Ohio's parentage statutes do not authorize this and the non-spousal artificial insemination statute does not apply to unmarried couples.
defendant_argument: The non-spousal artificial insemination statute should be interpreted gender-neutrally and applied retroactively to unmarried same-sex partners if they would have been married but for Ohio's unconstitutional ban on same-sex marriage, based on U.S. Supreme Court precedent (Obergefell and Pavan).
decision_outcome: The Ohio Supreme Court reversed the First District Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that Ohio's parentage statutes do not authorize a trial court to determine if an unmarried same-sex couple "would have been married" to apply the non-spousal artificial insemination statute.

title: State ex rel. Boggs v. City of Cleveland
description: Whether a property owner has standing to pursue a mandamus action to compel a foreign municipality to institute appropriation proceedings for compensation when the alleged taking occurred outside the municipality's corporate limits, with the plaintiff arguing they do have standing based on constitutional rights and the defendant arguing they do not due to lack of municipal authority outside its boundaries.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that she has standing because the Ohio Constitution guarantees compensation for private property taken for public use, regardless of whether the property is located within the taking municipality's jurisdiction, and that R.C. 719.01 allows a municipality to acquire property outside its jurisdiction for airport purposes.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the plaintiff lacked standing because a municipality has no authority to appropriate property outside its boundaries without specific statutory authorization, and that R.C. 719.01(O) does not apply to the plaintiff's property.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals, holding that Boggs has standing to pursue her mandamus claim, and remanded the case for consideration of the statute-of-limitations argument and then the merits of the taking claim.

title: Gatehouse Media Ohio Holdings v. City of Columbus Police Department
description: Whether police officers, when targeted by a criminal offender during a shootout while on duty, qualify as "victims" under Marsy's Law, thereby allowing their identifying information to be redacted from public records.
plaintiff_argument: The Dispatch contended that police officers, because they were on duty, cannot be "victims" under Marsy's Law and therefore their identifying information should not be redacted from public records.
defendant_argument: The Columbus Police Department (CPD) argued that the police officers involved in the shootout are "victims" under Marsy's Law, and thus their identifying information must be redacted from public records.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus, ruling that police officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their identifying information can be redacted from public records.

title: Lyon v. Riverside Methodist Hospital
description: Whether the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 is constitutional as applied to medical malpractice cases, with the plaintiff arguing it violates due process and equal protection, and the defendants arguing it is constitutional to stabilize healthcare costs.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 is unconstitutional as applied to her case, violating her rights to due process and equal protection.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 is constitutional and should be applied to limit noneconomic damages to stabilize healthcare costs and protect the medical profession.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, declaring the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 unconstitutional as applied to the plaintiff's case.

title: State ex rel. Martens v. Findlay Municipal Court
description: Whether George Martens had standing to bring a mandamus action challenging the jurisdiction of municipal courts over tax cases, specifically whether he could rely on the public-right doctrine or taxpayer standing.
plaintiff_argument: Martens argued he had standing based on the public-right doctrine, which allows litigants to bypass traditional standing requirements for issues of great public importance, or alternatively, as a taxpayer challenging the illegal expenditure of funds by courts.
defendant_argument: The Findlay Municipal Court and other appellees argued that Martens lacked standing to bring his complaint and failed to state a cognizable mandamus claim.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's dismissal of Martens' complaint, ruling that he lacked standing because the public-right doctrine (State ex rel. Ohio Academy of Trial Lawyers v. Sheward) was overruled, and he failed to establish taxpayer standing.

title: In Re Application for Correction of Birth Record of Hailey Emmeline Adelaide
description: Whether R.C. 3705.15 grants probate courts the authority to correct the sex marker on a transgender person's birth certificate.
plaintiff_argument: Adelaide argues that R.C. 3705.15 allows for the correction of the sex marker on her birth certificate to reflect her gender identity, and the probate court has the authority to grant this correction.
defendant_argument: The probate court and court of appeals denied Adelaide's application, concluding that R.C. 3705.15 only permits corrections for errors made at the time of birth, not amendments for later-in-life changes like gender identity.
decision_outcome: The court of appeals' judgment, which affirmed the probate court's denial of Adelaide's application to correct her sex marker, was left undisturbed due to the Supreme Court's inability to reach a majority decision.

title: Cincinnati Enquirer v. Bloom
description: Whether the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision prohibits the mandatory sealing of juvenile delinquency records without an individualized determination, thereby rendering R.C. 2151.356 unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The Cincinnati Enquirer argues that R.C. 2151.356 violates the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision by mandating the sealing of court records without balancing the public's interest against the juvenile's interest, and therefore seeks access to the sealed transcript.
defendant_argument: Judge Bloom argues that public access protections of the open courts provision do not apply to juvenile delinquency proceedings and that the Ohio Constitution provides no greater right of public access than the First Amendment, thus the statute mandating sealing is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court granted a writ of mandamus ordering Judge Bloom to provide access to the court records and a writ of prohibition precluding her from enforcing the order sealing the records, finding R.C. 2151.356 unconstitutional as applied without individualized determination.

title: Hild, Administration of the Estate of Boldman v. Samaritan Health Partners
description: Whether the "same-juror rule" or the "any-juror rule" applies in negligence cases, specifically regarding whether only jurors who find negligence may vote on the issue of proximate cause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the "same-juror rule" was erroneous and deprived her of the right to a full jury deliberation, advocating for the "any-juror rule" where all jurors could vote on proximate cause regardless of their negligence finding.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the "same-juror rule" logically applies to issues of negligence and proximate causation in medical negligence cases, and that courts must instruct juries to follow this rule.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Second District Court of Appeals' judgment, reinstated the trial court's denial of the plaintiff's motion for a new trial, and upheld the jury verdict in favor of the defendants.

title: State ex rel. Citizens Not Politicians v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether the ballot language and ballot title adopted by the Ohio Ballot Board and Secretary of State Frank LaRose for a proposed constitutional amendment on redistricting are misleading, deceptive, or defraud voters.
plaintiff_argument: The relators (Citizens Not Politicians and Ohio resident-electors) argue that the ballot language and ballot title are misleading, inaccurate, and constitute impermissible persuasive argument against the proposed amendment, thus violating constitutional standards.
defendant_argument: The Ohio Ballot Board and Secretary of State Frank LaRose argue that the ballot language and ballot title are factually accurate, properly identify the substance of the proposal, and do not amount to impermissible persuasive argument.
decision_outcome: The court granted a limited writ of mandamus, ordering the Secretary of State and Ohio Ballot Board to reconvene and adopt new ballot language for two specific sections, but denied the writ in all other respects regarding the ballot language and title.

title: State v. Carter
description: Whether a criminal defendant's Sixth Amendment right to face-to-face confrontation is violated when a witness testifies remotely via video conference without sufficient case-specific findings of necessity, and if so, whether such an error is harmless.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that remote testimony was justified due to increased COVID-19 spread and uncertain weather conditions, and that surging COVID-19 cases amounted to a public policy concern justifying the remote testimony.
defendant_argument: Eli Carter argued that the remote testimony of a witness via video conference, especially with speech-to-text captioning, violated his constitutional right to face-to-face confrontation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Third District Court of Appeals, concluding that while the trial court erred in allowing remote testimony, this error was harmless given the overwhelming evidence of guilt.

title: Smith v. Ohio State University
description: Whether discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar or an affirmative defense to suits brought against the state or its instrumentalities.
plaintiff_argument: Smith argued that discretionary immunity is an affirmative defense, meaning the Court of Claims has jurisdiction to hear the case and determine if immunity applies as a defense.
defendant_argument: Ohio State University argued that discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar, meaning the Court of Claims lacks subject-matter jurisdiction if immunity applies.
decision_outcome: The court held that discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar, not an affirmative defense, and reversed the Tenth District's judgment, remanding the case to determine if discretionary immunity applies to Ohio State's actions.

title: Schaad v. Alder
description: Whether the General Assembly violated the Due Process Clause by directing that an Ohio citizen pay taxes to the municipality of their principal place of work rather than their actual work location during the pandemic.
plaintiff_argument: Schaad argued that the temporary law violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by allowing a municipality to tax a nonresident for work performed outside that municipality.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Alder/Cincinnati) and lower courts argued that the law was constitutional, that municipalities can tax beyond their borders when permitted by state law, and that the law survived rational-basis review as it dealt with intrastate taxation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the temporary law (Section 29 of H.B. 197) was constitutional and a valid exercise of the General Assembly's authority.

title: Everhart v. Coshocton County Memorial Hospital
description: Whether the medical-claim statute of repose, R.C. 2305.113(C), applies to statutory wrongful-death claims.
plaintiff_argument: The medical-claim statute of repose does not apply to wrongful-death claims, as wrongful-death claims are distinct from medical malpractice claims and are governed by a separate statutory scheme.
defendant_argument: The medical-claim statute of repose applies to wrongful-death claims because the broad definition of "medical claim" in R.C. 2305.113(E)(3) clearly and unambiguously includes such claims.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Tenth District's decision, holding that the medical-claim statute of repose applies to statutory wrongful-death claims.

title: In re: Application of Alamo Solar I
description: Whether the Ohio Power Siting Board lawfully and reasonably granted certificates of environmental compatibility and public need for two large solar farms, despite claims of insufficient information regarding environmental impacts and inadequate mitigation measures.
plaintiff_argument: The Concerned Citizens of Preble County, L.L.C. argued that the Power Siting Board acted unlawfully and unreasonably by approving the solar farm applications without sufficient information on noise, visual impact, wildlife, flooding, stormwater runoff, and pollution, and by accepting inadequate setbacks.
defendant_argument: Alamo Solar I, L.L.C., Angelina Solar I, L.L.C., and the Power Siting Board argued that the board's orders granting certificates were lawful and reasonable, as the solar farms complied with statutory criteria and regulations, and the board's determinations were supported by evidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Power Siting Board's orders granting certificates for the construction of the solar facilities, finding that the citizens failed to establish that the board acted unlawfully or unreasonably.

title: State v. Daniel
description: Whether it violates the separation-of-powers doctrine to tie a judge's ability to reduce an arson offender's registration period to a recommendation from executive-branch officials.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Daniel, argued that the reduced-registration provision unconstitutionally infringed on the judicial power to impose a criminal sentence and limited judicial review by making a shortened registration period contingent on executive-branch recommendations.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Ohio, argued that the arson registration statute is not punitive and its requirements are not part of a criminal sentence, therefore it does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine.
decision_outcome: The Ohio Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Sixth District Court of Appeals, ruling that the arson-offender-registration scheme does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine.

title: League of Women Voters Ohio et al. v. Ohio Redistricting Commission et al.
description: Whether the Ohio Supreme Court should retain jurisdiction to review the constitutionality of the September 2023 General Assembly-districting plan, given its bipartisan support, or dismiss the cases and relinquish jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argued that the September 2023 plan, despite bipartisan approval, is a partisan gerrymander violating Article XI, Section 6(B) of the Ohio Constitution, and the court should retain jurisdiction to review it.
defendant_argument: Respondents argued that the bipartisan adoption of the September 2023 plan constitutes a changed circumstance, rendering the original complaints moot, and therefore the court should dismiss the cases and relinquish its continuing jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the cases, denied the motions to vacate as moot, and denied the petitioners' motions for leave to file objections to the September 2023 plan.

title: Bennett et al. v. Ohio Redistricting Commission et al.
description: Whether the Ohio Supreme Court should retain jurisdiction to review the constitutionality of the September 2023 General Assembly-districting plan, given its bipartisan support, or dismiss the cases and relinquish jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argued that the September 2023 plan, despite bipartisan approval, is a partisan gerrymander violating Article XI, Section 6(B) of the Ohio Constitution, and the court should retain jurisdiction to review it.
defendant_argument: Respondents argued that the bipartisan adoption of the September 2023 plan constitutes a changed circumstance, rendering the original complaints moot, and therefore the court should dismiss the cases and relinquish its continuing jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the cases, denied the motions to vacate as moot, and denied the petitioners' motions for leave to file objections to the September 2023 plan.

title: State ex rel. Ohioans United for Reproductive Rights v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether the ballot language adopted by the Ohio Ballot Board for a proposed constitutional amendment (Issue 1) is misleading, contains material omissions, or is improperly argumentative.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that the ballot language was misleading, contained material omissions, and was improperly argumentative, specifically citing the use of "citizens of the State" instead of "the State," "reproductive medical treatment" instead of "reproductive decisions," the omission of other reproductive decisions, and the use of terms like "unborn child" and absolute modifiers.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the ballot language properly identified the substance of the proposal, was not misleading, and was not improperly argumentative, asserting that "citizens of the State" is synonymous with "the State" in governmental power, and that other terms were factually accurate or imprecise but not misleading.
decision_outcome: The court granted a limited writ of mandamus, agreeing with the relators that the term "citizens of the State" in the ballot language was misleading and ordering the ballot board to change it to "the State." All other claims by the relators were denied.

title: Ohio Organizing Collaborative v. Ohio Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Ohio Supreme Court should retain jurisdiction to review the constitutionality of the September 2023 General Assembly-districting plan, given its bipartisan support, or dismiss the cases and relinquish jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argued that the September 2023 plan, despite bipartisan approval, is a partisan gerrymander violating Article XI, Section 6(B) of the Ohio Constitution, and the court should retain jurisdiction to review it.
defendant_argument: Respondents argued that the bipartisan adoption of the September 2023 plan constitutes a changed circumstance, rendering the original complaints moot, and therefore the court should dismiss the cases and relinquish its continuing jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the cases, denied the motions to vacate as moot, and denied the petitioners' motions for leave to file objections to the September 2023 plan.

title: State v. Hacker
description: Whether the Reagan Tokes Law's indefinite sentencing scheme is unconstitutional because it violates the separation-of-powers doctrine, the offender's right to a jury trial, and procedural due process.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants argued that the Reagan Tokes Law's indefinite sentencing scheme is unconstitutional as it violates the separation-of-powers doctrine, the right to a jury trial, and procedural due process.
defendant_argument: The appellee, the State of Ohio, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law is constitutional and does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine, the right to a jury trial, or procedural due process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgments of the Third and Eighth District Courts of Appeals, ruling that the Reagan Tokes Law is constitutional.

title: State ex rel. One Person One Vote v. LaRose
description: Whether the Ohio General Assembly may call for a special election on a legislatively-initiated constitutional amendment on any date, or if it is bound by existing statutes establishing when special elections may generally be held.
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly is bound by statutes (H.B. 458) that specify when special elections can be held, and the August 8 special election is not authorized by these laws, thus violating the Ohio Constitution and state law.
defendant_argument: Article XVI, Section 1 of the Ohio Constitution authorizes the General Assembly to "prescribe" a special election on a proposed constitutional amendment by joint resolution, allowing it to set the date without being bound by general election statutes.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus, ruling that the August 8, 2023 special election called by the General Assembly is constitutionally valid and can proceed.

title: The State ex rel. One Person One Vote v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether the ballot language and title adopted for a proposed constitutional amendment are incomplete and misleading, and whether the ballot board and Secretary of State should be compelled to adopt new, accurate language.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that the ballot language and title were incomplete and misleading because they failed to inform voters about current law, mischaracterized signature requirements, and used prejudicial language like "elevating standards" and "any constitutional amendment."
defendant_argument: The Ohio Ballot Board and Secretary of State Frank LaRose contended that the adopted ballot language and title properly identified the substance of the proposed amendment and were not misleading, deceptive, or fraudulent.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus in part, ordering the ballot board to adopt new language accurately defining "electors" for petition signatures and Secretary LaRose to remove the word "any" from the ballot title when referring to "constitutional amendment." The court denied the writ for other claims, including the need to describe current law or change the word "elevating."

title: State ex rel. DeBlase v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether an initiative petition proposing a constitutional amendment, titled "The Right to Reproductive Freedom with Protections for Health and Safety," contains a single proposed amendment or multiple, with the plaintiffs arguing it contains multiple amendments that should be divided, and the defendants arguing it contains only one.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the initiative petition contains more than one proposed constitutional amendment because it groups abortion with other reproductive decisions, claiming abortion is a unique act, and because it encompasses both broad constitutional language and specific legislative details.
defendant_argument: The defendants, the Ohio Ballot Board, determined that the initiative petition proposes a single constitutional amendment, as all its provisions relate to the single general purpose of protecting an individual's reproductive rights.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus, ruling that the Ohio Ballot Board did not abuse its discretion or disregard applicable law in determining that the initiative petition proposes only one constitutional amendment.

title: State ex rel. Ware v. Parikh
description: Whether an inmate's request for judges' oaths of office and specific court records should be granted under Ohio's Public Records Act, or if the oaths are governed by the Rules of Superintendence and the court records are exempt under R.C. 149.43(B)(8).
plaintiff_argument: Ware argued he was entitled to both categories of records under the Public Records Act and sought a writ of mandamus.
defendant_argument: Parikh argued the oaths were governed by the Rules of Superintendence, not the Public Records Act, and the other court records were exempt under R.C. 149.43(B)(8) because they related to a criminal investigation/prosecution case initiated before July 1, 2009.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus in part, ordering the clerk to produce the requested records from the Cincinnati Enquirer case and awarding Ware $1,000 in statutory damages and court costs, but denied the writ for the judges' oaths of office.

title: Brandt v. Pompa
description: Whether the compensatory-damages caps for noneconomic loss in R.C. 2315.18 are unconstitutional as applied to appellant, Amanda Brandt, with Brandt arguing they are unconstitutional and Pompa arguing they are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The statutory caps on noneconomic damages (R.C. 2315.18) are unconstitutional as applied to her case, particularly because they exclude severe psychological injuries from exceptions, are arbitrary for victims of intentional criminal acts, and violate her rights to due process, jury trial, open courts, and a remedy.
defendant_argument: The statutory caps on noneconomic damages (R.C. 2315.18) are constitutional as applied, as they serve a legitimate government interest in protecting the state's economy and addressing the subjective nature of noneconomic damages, and Brandt's injuries do not fall under the statutory exceptions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio held that R.C. 2315.18, which caps noneconomic damages, is unconstitutional as applied to Brandt and similarly situated plaintiffs who suffer permanent and severe psychological injuries from intentional criminal acts, reversing the appellate court's judgment and reinstating the jury's original damages verdict.

title: McClain v. State
description: Whether a defendant is entitled to a jury trial under Article I, Section 5 of the Ohio Constitution in a claim for wrongful imprisonment, with the plaintiff arguing for the right to a jury trial and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: McClain argues that a wrongful-imprisonment claim has roots in the common law in the intentional tort of false imprisonment, which carried with it a right to a jury trial, and therefore he is entitled to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The state argues that McClain's claim is statutory, has no common-law analogue, seeks relief unavailable at common law, and that the state cannot be sued at common law without its express consent, meaning the statute created a new cause of action without displacing former remedies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the First District Court of Appeals, holding that Anthony McClain has no constitutional right to a jury trial in his action to be declared a wrongfully imprisoned person under R.C. 2743.48 because this type of action did not exist at common law.

title: State v. Brasher
description: Whether a trial court retains jurisdiction to impose restitution on a defendant after the defendant has completed their prison sentence and the original sentencing judgment has become final, or if victims must appeal the initial denial of restitution directly.
plaintiff_argument: Victims are constitutionally entitled to full and timely restitution under Marsy's Law and should have an effective appellate remedy, including seeking a writ of mandamus, even after the defendant's sentence is completed.
defendant_argument: The trial court loses jurisdiction to modify a sentence once it is final and the defendant has completed their prison term, and imposing restitution afterward violates Double Jeopardy. Victims should have pursued a direct appeal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgment of the Twelfth District Court of Appeals, ruling that the trial court's later order of restitution was void because it lacked jurisdiction to modify the sentence after it became final and the defendant had completed his prison term.

title: State v. Morris
description: Whether a trial court that sentences a juvenile defendant to life in prison without considering their youth as a mitigating factor violates the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution and Article I, Section 9 of the Ohio Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Morris argued that the trial court failed to consider his youth as a mitigating factor in sentencing, which constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under both the Ohio and federal constitutions, as required by *State v. Patrick*.
defendant_argument: The Ohio Attorney General (amicus curiae for the state) argued that neither the United States Constitution nor the Ohio Constitution requires a trial court to consider a juvenile offender's age on the record before sentencing to a life sentence with parole, and that *Jones v. Mississippi* effectively overruled *State v. Patrick*.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the Fifth District Court of Appeals, holding that Morris's sentence constitutes cruel and unusual punishment, and remanded the case to the trial court to vacate the sentence and resentence him after considering his youth as a mitigating factor.

title: In re D.R.
description: Whether R.C. 2152.84, which mandates continued Tier I sex offender classification for 16- and 17-year-old juvenile offenders without judicial discretion at the completion-of-disposition hearing, violates due process.
plaintiff_argument: D.R. argues that R.C. 2152.84 is unconstitutional as applied to him because it removes judicial discretion to terminate his sex offender classification at the completion-of-disposition hearing, violating his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The state argues that R.C. 2152.84 is fundamentally fair and complies with due process, as it provides an initial classification hearing with discretion and allows for a review to terminate registration after three years.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's decision, ruling that R.C. 2152.84(A)(2)(b) is unconstitutional as applied to D.R. because it removes judicial discretion at the completion-of-disposition hearing, violating due process. The case was remanded for a new hearing.

title: State v. Haynes
description: Whether a criminal defendant has a mandatory right to a bill of particulars upon timely request, even when the state provides open-file discovery.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio (appellee) argued that a bill of particulars is not required when open-file discovery is provided, and that the defendant was not prejudiced as all necessary information was available through discovery.
defendant_argument: Haynes (appellant) argued he had a constitutional and statutory right to a bill of particulars to understand the specific charges and conduct alleged, which was not sufficiently clear from the indictment or discovery, thus hampering his defense.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the Sixth District Court of Appeals, vacated Haynes's conviction, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Yerkey
description: Whether a crime victim is entitled to receive restitution from an offender for wages lost as a result of the victim's choice to exercise her right to attend court hearings.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio argued that Marsy's Law provides a constitutional right to full and timely restitution, which includes lost wages incurred by victims attending court proceedings.
defendant_argument: John Yerkey argued that restitution in Ohio law is limited to economic losses directly and proximately caused by the offense, and lost wages for voluntarily attending court hearings do not qualify.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgment of the Seventh District Court of Appeals, ruling that lost wages incurred by a victim for attending court hearings are not compensable as restitution under Ohio law.

title: State ex rel. Maras v. LaRose
description: Whether R.C. 3505.21, which governs election observers, is unconstitutional for requiring independent candidates to form a group of five to appoint observers and for not allowing observers to inspect vote-tabulating machine software and source codes.
plaintiff_argument: Maras contends R.C. 3505.21 violates Equal Protection by treating independent candidates differently from political parties regarding election observers and that observers need access to vote-tabulating machine software/source codes for meaningful observation.
defendant_argument: Secretary LaRose argues R.C. 3505.21 is constitutional under rational-basis review, as it applies equally to all candidates and serves a legitimate government interest in minimizing disruptions. He also argues the court cannot create a new legal duty for software inspection.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus, upholding the constitutionality of R.C. 3505.21 and refusing to compel the Secretary of State to allow independent candidates to appoint observers without the five-candidate rule or to provide access to vote-tabulating machine software/source codes.

title: State ex rel. Sanduskians for Sandusky v. The City of Sandusky
description: Whether a municipal charter-amendment petition must comply with the full-text requirement of R.C. 731.31 to be submitted to the electors.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that R.C. 731.31 does not apply to charter-amendment petitions, and therefore their petition, despite not containing the full text, should be certified for a vote.
defendant_argument: The city respondents argued that the relators' petition was insufficient in form because it did not contain the full text of the proposed amendment, as required by R.C. 731.31.
decision_outcome: The court granted a limited writ of mandamus, ordering the city commission to enact an ordinance to submit the proposed charter amendment to the electors at a special election, provided the petition has enough valid signatures, but denied the request for placement on the November 8, 2022 ballot and attorney fees.

title: Neiman v. LaRose
description: Whether the March 2 congressional-district plan unduly favors a political party or its incumbents and unduly splits governmental units, violating Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) and (b) of the Ohio Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The March 2 plan unduly favors the Republican Party and disfavors the Democratic Party, and unduly splits governmental units, violating Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) and (b) of the Ohio Constitution.
defendant_argument: The March 2 plan is constitutional, complies with Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) and (b), and reasonably attempts to maximize competitive seats, arguing that Section 1(C)(3) does not apply to remedial plans adopted by the commission.
decision_outcome: The court held that the March 2 plan does not comply with Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) of the Ohio Constitution and is therefore invalid, ordering the General Assembly to pass a new plan within 30 days.

title: State ex rel. Demora v. LaRose
description: Whether the statutory filing deadlines for primary election candidates automatically shifted when a federal court ordered a new primary election date, or if the original deadlines remained in effect.
plaintiff_argument: The original relators argued that statutory filing deadlines are tied to the actual primary election date, and since the August 2 primary was set, their declarations filed in May were timely according to R.C. 3513.05 and 3513.041.
defendant_argument: Secretary LaRose argued that the original February filing deadlines remained in effect, and the federal court order moving the primary date did not reopen or alter these deadlines, making later filings untimely and void.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus for the original relators, compelling the Secretary of State and county boards of elections to accept their declarations of candidacy and petitions as timely and certify them to the August 2 primary ballot if they otherwise qualify. The court denied the writ of mandamus for the intervening relators.

title: The Village of Newburgh Heights v. State
description: Whether the Ohio Constitution's Home Rule Amendment prohibits the General Assembly from enacting statutes that reduce a municipality's local-government fund share based on traffic camera fines and require an advance deposit for civil actions to enforce traffic camera citations.
plaintiff_argument: The municipalities argued that the state's spending setoff and deposit requirement unconstitutionally infringe on their home-rule powers to enforce traffic laws with cameras, claiming it would compel them to abandon traffic camera use.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the General Assembly's discretionary spending power and the challenged traffic camera law provisions (spending setoff and deposit requirement) do not violate the Ohio Constitution's Home Rule Amendment.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate court's judgment, ruling that the spending setoff and deposit requirement do not violate the municipalities' home-rule authority, and remanded the case.

title: State v. McAlpin
description: Whether Joseph McAlpin's convictions and death sentence should be affirmed despite his claims of violations of his right to self-representation, interference by standby counsel, improper admission of evidence, prosecutorial misconduct, erroneous jury instructions, and the constitutionality of the death penalty.
plaintiff_argument: McAlpin argues that his trial and sentencing were fundamentally unfair and unconstitutional due to multiple errors, including the denial of his right to control his defense, prejudicial evidence, and flawed jury instructions, warranting the reversal of his convictions and death sentence.
defendant_argument: The State argues that McAlpin received a fair trial, that any alleged errors were either forfeited or non-prejudicial, and that the evidence overwhelmingly supported his guilt and the imposition of the death penalty.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed Joseph McAlpin's convictions and death sentence.

title: Siltstone Res. v. Ohio Public Works Commission
description: Whether the transfer restriction in the deed for property acquired with public funds for conservation is an enforceable and valid restraint on alienation, with the plaintiff arguing it is an invalid restraint on alienation and the defendant arguing it is valid and enforceable due to its public and charitable purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The transfer restriction is an invalid and unreasonable restraint on alienation, and therefore unenforceable, meaning the transfers of subsurface mineral rights should be upheld.
defendant_argument: The transfer restriction is valid, reasonable, and enforceable because it serves a charitable or public purpose of land conservation and preservation, and the state is entitled to remedies for its violation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Seventh District Court of Appeals, holding that the transfer restriction in the deed was valid and that the transfer of mineral interests violated these restrictions, entitling the state to relief.

title: Adams v. DeWine
description: Whether the congressional-district plan passed by the General Assembly unduly favors or disfavors a political party or its incumbents and unduly splits governmental units, violating Article XIX of the Ohio Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The congressional-district plan unduly favors the Republican Party and unduly splits urban counties for partisan advantage, violating Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) and (b) of the Ohio Constitution.
defendant_argument: The congressional-district plan is constitutional, as the General Assembly prioritized creating competitive districts and complied with Article XIX's rules on splitting governmental units, and does not unduly favor a political party.
decision_outcome: The court declared the congressional-district plan invalid and ordered the General Assembly to pass a new plan that complies with Article XIX of the Ohio Constitution.

title: DuBose v. McGuffey
description: Whether the $1,500,000 bail set by the trial court for Justin DuBose was unconstitutionally excessive, and whether the court of appeals correctly applied a de novo standard of review or should have applied an abuse-of-discretion standard.
plaintiff_argument: DuBose argued that the $1,500,000 bail was excessive, effectively denying him bail, as it did not consider his financial resources, and he presented evidence to counter the flight risk claim.
defendant_argument: The state argued that the court of appeals erred by applying de novo review instead of abuse of discretion, and by disregarding the victim's family's safety concerns, maintaining the $1,500,000 bail was appropriate given the serious charges and flight risk.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeals' judgment, which reduced Justin DuBose's bail from $1,500,000 to $500,000, finding the original amount unconstitutionally excessive.

title: The Cleveland Electric Illuminating Co. v. The City of Cleveland
description: Whether a municipality violates Article XVIII, Section 6 of the Ohio Constitution by selling an "artificial surplus" of electricity to customers outside its boundaries, where the plaintiff argues it does and the defendant argues it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Cleveland Electric Illuminating Co. (CEI), argues that the city's extraterritorial sale of electricity constitutes an "artificial surplus" acquired solely for resale beyond city limits, which violates the Ohio Constitution and prior court decisions.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the City of Cleveland, argues that Article XVIII, Section 6 allows municipalities to sell surplus electricity extraterritorially and that it may acquire excess capacity for legitimate reasons (e.g., cost, risk mitigation, reserve margins) other than solely for extraterritorial resale.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Eighth District Court of Appeals' judgment, which reversed the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the city and remanded the case for further proceedings to determine the purpose of the city's electricity purchases.

title: State ex rel. Suwalski v. Peeler
description: Whether Judge Peeler had the judicial power to relieve Roy Ewing of his federal firearms disability, and whether Jamie Suwalski, as a crime victim, had the right to challenge this restoration under Marsy's Law.
plaintiff_argument: Suwalski argued that Judge Peeler lacked the judicial power to restore Ewing's federal firearms rights and that his order violated her rights as a crime victim under Marsy's Law, thus warranting a writ of prohibition.
defendant_argument: Ewing contended that Suwalski failed to exhaust her claims, Marsy's Law was inapplicable, the action was barred by res judicata, and Judge Peeler had the statutory authority to restore his firearms rights under state and federal law, making a writ of prohibition unwarranted.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' judgment, granting a writ of prohibition that invalidated Judge Peeler's order restoring Ewing's federal firearms rights.

title: State v. Jordan
description: Whether a police officer is constitutionally required to secure an arrest warrant before conducting a public felony arrest when it is practicable to do so.
plaintiff_argument: Jordan argued that a warrantless arrest is unconstitutional if there is an unreasonable delay in effecting the arrest, or if it was practicable to obtain a warrant.
defendant_argument: The State argued that a warrantless arrest based on probable cause in a public place does not violate the Fourth Amendment, and neither exigent circumstances nor impracticability of obtaining a warrant is necessary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the First District Court of Appeals, holding that a warrantless public arrest based on probable cause is constitutionally valid and does not require exigent circumstances or impracticability of obtaining a warrant.

title: State v. Hubbard
description: Whether the retroactive application of "Sierah's Law" to offenders who committed their offenses prior to the law's effective date violates the Retroactivity Clause of the Ohio Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is remedial and the defendant arguing it is punitive.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio argued that Sierah's Law is remedial, not punitive, and therefore its retroactive application does not violate the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause, as it does not impair vested rights or impose new burdens.
defendant_argument: Hubbard argued that Sierah's Law imposes new, punitive burdens, duties, obligations, and liabilities that did not exist at the time he committed his offense, thereby violating the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Twelfth District Court of Appeals, ruling that the retroactive application of Sierah's Law does not violate the Retroactivity Clause of the Ohio Constitution.
